subject: Forensic log retention & residency — post-incident Q&A
messages:

Cc: security@acme-corp.com

Subject: Questions on log retention & residency after outage

Hi Hannah / Marissa,

Thanks again for the post-incident summary you shared this morning. The Acme security team has a couple of follow-ups to close our internal evidence package for the outage:

- For forensic purposes, how long will Redwood retain raw request logs, debug traces, and kernel-level telemetry after the incident?
- Do any of those artifacts leave the region (we're particularly concerned about EU-sourced data)?
- If we request an export for our audit, what format & chain-of-custody metadata do you provide, and how soon can we expect the export?

We may need a signed statement for procurement. Could you point us to the runbook or provide an export sample?

Appreciate a short, actionable reply.

—Jane
Jane Doe
Lead InfoSec
Acme Corp
From: Hannah Schmitt <hannah.schmitt@redwood.com>
To: Jane Doe <jane.doe@acme-corp.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>, Vivek Kulkarni <vivek.kulkarni@redwood.com>
Date: Mon, 10 Aug 2026 11:02:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Questions on log retention & residency after outage

Hi Jane — thanks for flagging these specific asks. Quick answers up front, then Vivek will follow with the forensic specifics and artifacts:

- Default retention: access/request logs (90 days), debug/traces (30 days), kernel-level telemetry and perf traces (14 days).
- Incident preservation: for incidents we snapshot raw artifacts and extend retention for the case — typically 180 days for request logs and 90 days for traces, unless legal hold or escalation requires longer.
- Residency: artifacts are stored in the same region as the customer workload by default. If we replicated any artifacts during cross-region failover, we will note that in the export.
- Exports: we can provide encrypted tarball exports (SHA256 checksummed) with accompanying manifest and chain-of-custody metadata. Timeline: standard request turnaround is 3 business days; for incident-critical exports we can prioritize within 24–48 hours.

I'm looping in Vivek to provide the runbook link, the exact list of preserved files, and the typical manifest we attach.

Thanks,

Hannah Schmitt

Hi Jane — Vivek from Redwood Security. Sorry for the longer note but wanted to capture specifics so your auditors have what they need. Below is our typical post-incident forensic handling (Ive included the manifest and a sanitized snapshot as attachments):

1) Classes of artifacts we preserve
   - API/request logs (raw HTTP headers, timestamps, route, model id) — preserved as gzip CSVs.
   - Engine traces / tokenizer events — preserved as binary trace files (diagnostic format).
   - Kernel/perf telemetry (GPU memory maps, scheduling events) — preserved when collected; typically smaller sets.
   - Controller logs (autoscaler, routing decisions) — plain text logs.
   - KV-cache snapshots (when relevant to request reconstruction) — stored encrypted and hashed.

2) Retention policy for incident exports
   - Standard: request logs 90d, traces 30d, perf 14d.
   - Post-incident snapshot: request logs 180d, traces 90d, perf 30d (subject to legal hold extension).

3) Residency & replication
   - Default storage follows the customer region (US, EU, APAC).
   - If cross-region failover occurred during the incident we mark any replicas and include their locations in the manifest.
   - All stored artifacts are encrypted at rest using customer-segregated keys where requested (KMS/HSM integration available for Private deployments).

4) Export format & chain-of-custody
   - Exports are provided as encrypted tar.gz with: 
       * manifest.csv (file list, SHA256, generation timestamps, source host IDs)
       * chain_of_custody.txt (who accessed/packaged the export, purpose, and retention lift)
       * redaction_report.txt (if PII was redacted)
   - We include a signed metadata blob (PKCS7) and SHA256 so you can verify integrity.
   - Transfer: S3 pre-signed URL with limited TTL or secure transfer to a customer SFTP endpoint; we can also ship encrypted disk under exceptional legal requests.

5) Chain-of-custody process
   - Only authorized security engineers perform export packaging; a second engineer performs checksum and signs the export.
   - We log export creation in an immutable audit trail.

6) Deletion after export / legal hold
   - Normal deletion flows proceed after the extended retention window unless you place a legal hold. If Acme requests deletion, we will provide a deletion certificate listing file hashes and deletion timestamps.

7) Timeline & point of contact
   - For this incident we can prioritize an export within 24 hours. I attached a sample manifest and a sanitized snapshot of non-sensitive logs for your review.

Attachments: forensic_evidence_manifest.csv (manifest sample), incident_snapshot-20260810.tgz (sanitized sample)

If you need a formal signed attestation for procurement, we can prepare a one-page statement that describes these commitments and timelines — I'll work with Legal for that.

Regards,

Vivek Kulkarni
Head of Security & Compliance, Redwood Inference

Jane — thanks for the fast turnaround on questions. Short commercial summary so procurement has what it needs:

- Commitment: Redwood will preserve a prioritized incident snapshot (request logs + traces) for 180 days, stored in Acme's primary region, with SHA256 checksums and a chain-of-custody manifest.
- Export options: encrypted tarball via S3 presigned link (standard) or secure SFTP delivery.
- Turnaround: 24–72 hours depending on prioritization; we will treat this incident as high priority.

Next steps: Hannah will send a procurement-friendly one-page attestation and a DocuSign if you need a signed commitment. Vivek will deliver the artifacts and manifest to the Drive link below.
